summary: Japan's everyday green tea: leaves are steamed shortly after picking, which halts oxidation quickly and preserves a vivid green color, then rolled into fine needles and dried. Steaming (rather than the pan-firing used in China) gives sencha its characteristic vegetal, grassy-sweet flavor.

A shaded green tea: the bushes are covered for roughly the last three weeks before harvest, which lowers catechin (bitterness) production and raises theanine, giving gyokuro an intensely savory, sweet, umami-rich character quite unlike sun-grown sencha. Traditionally brewed with a lot of leaf and very little, cool water.

Shade-grown tea leaves (tencha) that are steamed, dried, and stone-ground into a fine powder, then whisked directly into water rather than steeped and strained. Central to Japanese tea ceremony (chanoyu). Flavor is intensely vegetal and umami, with body and bitterness varying widely by grade.

Green tea, typically bancha or sencha leaf and stems, roasted at high heat after processing. Roasting turns the leaf reddish-brown and destroys most of the catechins responsible for bitterness, giving hojicha a toasty, nutty, low-caffeine cup that tolerates near-boiling water well.

Sencha or bancha leaf blended with roasted, popped brown rice (genmai). Originating in the Edo period as a way for merchants to stretch scarce tea leaf, it became a household staple during wartime and postwar shortages. The rice mellows the cup and adds a nutty, toasted-grain flavor alongside the tea's vegetal notes; caffeine content is lower than straight sencha simply because leaf makes up less of the blend.

The everyday, lower grade of Japanese green tea, made from the larger, more mature leaves of later summer or autumn harvests rather than the tender spring flush used for sencha. It is steamed and processed the same way as sencha, but mature leaf develops fewer catechins, giving bancha a milder, drier, less vegetal cup with far less astringency and bitterness than sencha or shaded teas.

Twig tea: the stems, stalks, and leaf ribs sorted out during the final refinement of sencha or gyokuro, rather than a leaf picked and processed on its own. Because stems receive less sunlight on the growing plant, they accumulate fewer catechins, giving kukicha a notably sweet, creamy, low-astringency cup with a soft woody aroma. Stem tea sorted from gyokuro production is sometimes sold separately as the more prized "karigane".

A shade-grown green tea positioned between sencha and gyokuro: the bushes are covered with cloth laid directly over the canopy (jikagake) for roughly one to two weeks before harvest, a shorter and less complete shading than gyokuro's elevated tana frames. The result carries more umami and sweetness than unshaded sencha without the intense, broth-like character of gyokuro.

Deep-steamed sencha: the kill-green steaming step runs 60 seconds or longer, roughly double the time used for standard sencha, which softens the leaf and breaks it into smaller fragments during rolling. The longer steaming lowers astringency and produces a fuller, sweeter, more full-bodied cup, but it also releases more fine particles into the liquor, giving fukamushicha its characteristically cloudy, deep-green brew.

Also called guricha, a green tea processed like sencha except for the final shaping step, which is skipped; without it the leaf dries into loose curls and coils rather than straight needles. The steamed version (mushisei) was developed in 1925 to mimic the pan-fired teas Russian buyers preferred for export, while a pan-fired version (kamairi) also exists. Skipping the shaping step reduces cell damage, giving tamaryokucha a milder, less astringent cup than sencha.

A rare exception among Japanese greens: instead of steaming, the leaf is fired in a hot iron pan (up to around 300°C) to halt oxidation, the same basic approach used for most Chinese green tea. Produced mainly in Kyushu (Ureshino in Saga, and the Aoyagi style of Kumamoto and Miyazaki), pan-firing leaves out the grassy, marine notes steaming produces and gives kamairicha a mellow, sweet cup with a light roasted aroma and little astringency.

A sencha-style green tea from Saitama, traditionally named alongside Shizuoka and Uji as one of Japan's three great teas, per the old saying "color is Shizuoka, aroma is Uji, taste is Sayama" (色は静岡、香りは宇治、味は狭山). What sets it apart is not a different base process but its finishing roast, Sayama hi-ire, developed in 1802 and run hotter than standard sencha firing; it was devised to dry out the unusually thick leaves the region's cold winters and frost-prone climate produce. The deeper roast gives Sayama-cha a nutty, toasty sweetness and body beyond typical sencha.

The season's first-flush sencha: leaf picked at the very start of harvest (from late March in the south to May further north) and rushed to market fresh rather than blended with or aged alongside later pickings. Winter dormancy lets the youngest leaves accumulate more theanine and less catechin than later flushes, giving shincha a sweeter, more delicate, less astringent cup than standard sencha from the same garden. It is sold as a limited, dated seasonal release, with its own devoted yearly following rather than any single growing region to call its own.

The fine leaf particles and dust sifted out during the final refinement of sencha and gyokuro, rather than leaf grown and processed on its own — the same waste-nothing logic that produces kukicha from stems, applied here to fragments. The small particle size infuses quickly into a strong, brisk cup, which is why konacha, served under the name agari, is the tea most commonly poured free at sushi restaurants to cut the richness of fish between courses.

The tightly curled young buds and shoot tips separated out during sencha and gyokuro refinement because they don't roll into the long, straight needles graders require, rather than leaf harvested and processed as its own crop. Because buds concentrate more of the plant's compounds than mature leaf, mecha brews stronger, more astringent, and more deeply umami than the sencha it was sorted from, at a lower price than the parent grade.

Made by parboiling coarse summer leaf, then packing it while still hot into barrels under a weighted lid, where anaerobic lactic-acid bacteria ferment it for two to several weeks before it is sun-dried — a wholly different process from the steaming or pan-firing used for green tea, closer to pickling than to conventional tea-making. The lactic fermentation lowers catechins, caffeine, and theanine while raising lactic and other organic acids, giving awa bancha a distinctly sour, tangy, faintly effervescent cup unlike any steamed sencha. Produced traditionally around Kamikatsu and Naka in Tokushima, it is listed on Slow Food's Ark of Taste.

Undergoes two separate fermentations rather than a single kill-green step: leaves are steamed, then spread on straw mats for about a week of aerobic mold fermentation, then packed into barrels for weeks of anaerobic bacterial fermentation, before being pressed into blocks, cut into small squares, and sun-dried on straw mats — a process closer to aged pu-erh than to any green tea. The dried squares resemble the black stones (goishi) of the board game go, giving the tea its name. Production has for centuries been confined to the mountain town of Otoyo in Kochi; the method was recognized as an Intangible Cultural Property of Japan in 2018, and it yields a smooth, mildly sour, mellow cup with little of green tea's astringency.

Like goishicha, it undergoes a two-stage fermentation rather than steaming: leaves are first left to ferment aerobically until coated in a white "noble mold," then packed tightly into barrels for about two weeks of anaerobic bacterial fermentation before drying. Produced only around Mount Ishizuchi in Ehime, using a method dating to the Edo period that nearly died out in 1996 when a single farmer remained who knew it, the tea yields a fresh, fruity, plum-like acidity distinct from both green tea and from the milder goishicha.

Bancha-grade leaf undergoes roughly a month of aerobic koji-mold fermentation, with no lactic-acid stage, then is dried and traditionally boiled rather than steeped — a mold-driven fermentation, and a boiled rather than infused preparation, both unlike any steamed Japanese green tea. A pinch of salt is added to the boiled liquor, which is then whisked into a stable foam with a double-headed bamboo whisk (batabatachasen); the back-and-forth whisking motion gives the tea its onomatopoeic name. The tradition, centered on the village of Birudan in Toyama's Asahi district, is recorded as far back as 1472.

Japan's own black tea, fully oxidized rather than steamed like sencha, developed from the 1870s as a Meiji-era export crop meant to compete with Chinese, Indian, and Ceylon black teas — production even drew on Assam seed stock a Japanese delegation brought back from India in 1876. Made mostly from Japanese cultivars bred for green tea's low tannin and high theanine rather than from Assam-type bushes, wakoucha comes out lighter, sweeter, and less astringent than Indian or Sri Lankan black teas, usually without the malty bitterness typical of the style. Export demand collapsed after trade liberalization in 1971, and today wakoucha is a small-scale specialty made in Shizuoka, Miyazaki, and other prefectures rather than an export commodity.
